source: Somsak Wannasaree, "Banana Orchards" (Thai original, Rural Agriculture Printing House, Nonthaburi, Jan 1989), Khmer translation for Battambang Provincial Dept. of Agriculture / Cambodia NW Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee, funded by SEILA Programme, 1st printing Jan 1997, section 2 (botanical classification)
text:
Banana belongs to the family Musaceae, which contains two genera: Ensete (non-fruiting ornamental/wild types) and Musa, the genus that includes essentially all cultivated edible bananas. Most edible cultivated varieties are triploid (carrying three sets of chromosomes rather than the normal two), which is the underlying reason they are seedless: triploid plants generally cannot complete normal seed formation, so the fruit develops through parthenocarpy (fruit swelling without fertilization) instead. This is why commercial banana varieties reliably produce seedless fruit and must be propagated vegetatively (via suckers) rather than from seed.

By contrast, some wild and a few cultivated banana types are diploid (two sets of chromosomes) and, when pollinated, can produce viable seed; true wild seeded bananas (sometimes eaten only for their young shoots, or kept for breeding purposes) can carry many hard, dark seeds packed densely in the flesh, which makes them unpalatable as fresh fruit compared to seedless cultivated types. Understanding this distinction is useful mainly for explaining why nearly all farmer-grown banana varieties must be multiplied from suckers or corm pieces rather than seed, and why an occasional seed found in an otherwise seedless variety's fruit is not unusual biologically.
